written_by_MFA011.Excerpt1: I’d spoken with Reva last week, but it was a short conversation filled mostly with platitudes. She’d seemed distracted and said she was at the gym. When the news broke about the towers, I called her a few times, but she didn’t pick up. Without thinking, I went immediately to the store to purchase a TV/VCR machine. Suddenly the most important thing was to record all the news footage that was blaring at me from out of my TV. I thought briefly about calling Trevor, then remembered that he was in Barbados on his honeymoon, probably sipping a drink with some spiky, inedible part of a fruit in it, completely unaware of what had happened. Once the sun went down and I still hadn’t heard from her, I realized that Reva was lost, likely for good. For days I sat watching and rewatching the footage I’d taped of the attacks, unable to move from in front of the TV save to piss or search the bathroom cabinet for more pills. There was a video of a woman leaping from the North Tower, and though it was too grainy for me to ever be able to tell if it was Reva, I liked imagining that it was.She wore a grey pencil skirt with black tights and stilettos – one still gripping her foot while the other had torn free, suspended in the air. She looked so beautiful, jumping like that into the unknown, that I took a kind of strange and holy comfort in her courage.
written_by_MFA011.Excerpt2: "You should hang out more," I told Reva. "You'd like that, huh?" I could hear the whir of the machines in the background. "I gotta go, weirdo. I'm at the gym."On the morning of September 11, 2001, I went straight from the bodega where I got my coffee to Circuit City and charged a new TV/VCR combo on my Visa to record the news coverage. Trevor was on his honeymoon in Barbados. Everything was happening as it was supposed to. Reva was now "lost." For a full week I watched the same footage of the planes hitting the Twin Towers, the burning people plummeting, the buildings crumbling at the end like collapsing sand castles from every angle the news had to show.One woman leapt from a window from the North Tower and somehow caught my attention. She had on a skirt or a dress and was barefoot. As she spun, her stockings caught the updraft like sails, and I could see the outline of her thighs. She fell so gracefully. It looked almost like she was dancing. If I squinted, she looked like Reva. Of course I loved her—I had spent the last year mourning her as though she were dead. But I didn't cry. I wasn't hurt. I didn't feel sad. I just admired her, looked up at her there, so far above me and so elegant.
written_by_MFA011.Reason: Excerpt 1 flows better and shows greater complexity behind the relationship. Excerpt 2 is not as astutely descriptive as Excerpt 1. In Excerpt 2, the narrator states "She fell so gracefully," and in Excerpt 1, the moment is described as "She looked so beautiful, jumping like that into the unknown, that I took a kind of strange and holy comfort in her courage." Therefore, Excerpt 1 is more rooted in the point of view than Excerpt 2.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: The last time I spoke to Reva, she was distant. Eager to get back to sweating on the elliptical, or stair-master, or whatever absurd machine she was convinced would keep away the horrors of arm flab. She’s distant now, too, but in a new way. That day, Trevor was on his honeymoon in Barbados, but Reva felt farther. She was gone, lost. I still feel a faint throb of theft when I think of them. On the morning of September 11th , I bought a TV/VCR and recorded the towers going down. When I find myself drifting, floating back to the state I had been in that previous year, I turn on the recording and watch. The footage isn’t soothing, it’s scalding—it wakes me up and keeps me conscious. In one clip, my favorite clip, a woman leaps from a window ledge in the North Tower. She looks enough like Reva that if I were feeling sentimental, I could pretend it’s her. The edge of her pencil skirt whipping up could be Reva’s knock-off designer, her shoes flying from her feet and floating up past her head could be Reva’s second hand Manolos, the glints of sunlight that could be Reva’s grandmother’s ring. But it doesn’t have to be. I don’t need her to be Reva. In dreams, when you feel like you’re falling, you jolt awake. I need her to wake me up.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: Reva seemed distant the last time we talked, though maybe I’m just imagining that now. She was breathing heavily into the phone when she picked up. It sounded like she was having sex, and I made a mean joke about it, and she laughed in a forced way and told me she was at the gym, on the elliptical, which I could imagine easily, her in that ugly little workout set, climbing toward nothing. She told me she’d call me back later, but she never did. Then she went missing after 9/11, and I knew she was dead. Not in any kind of mystical or spiritual way, but because I knew there was no other option. That same day, I bought a TV/VCR from Best Buy with cash because I wanted to record the news coverage. Now, I watch it, not in a morbid way, but hoping I’ll find a clue, about something, maybe about Reva, maybe about something else. It’s not about Trevor anymore. He’s in Barbados on his honeymoon, probably slathering sunscreen on his anorexic wife and pretending to be happy. Or maybe he is happy. I was watching one of the recordings today when I spotted something. From the smoking North Tower, a woman poked her torso out of a window. She was wearing a blue sweater and jeans. She had brown hair, short like Reva’s. She hovered on the edge for a moment, then let go and plunged into the unknown. She sailed weightlessly through the air, and then she disappeared out of frame.

The gym phone call happens at an unspecified time before 9/11 (immediately before?) and the conversation is rather generic. It's not clear why "Everything was happening as it was supposed to" or what "Reva was now 'lost'" means. Then, because the narrator compares Reva to a woman who jumps from the Twin Towers, it sounds as if Reva died on 9/11, but the narrator states that she's been mourning Reva "for a year" when 9/11, in this excerpt, happened the previous week. The second excerpt is much clearer: Reva and the narrator have an entertaining, cruel friendship; Reva went missing in 9/11; and the narrator obsessively watches the footage, hoping to see her.

written_by_MFA001.Excerpt1: That Saturday morning the light was orange through the window in his uncle's garage, bouncing off against the car, making the red paint seem redder. His uncle's ghost had made an appearance in the man's dream last night, making woosh-whee-whooo sounds. There were also smears of blood and the sound of the last scream of the man he had killed. The former premier. A Nouveu Fascist, the worst kind you could be, other than a Neo-Nouveu Fascist, which was much worse. The dreams had started after the pull of the gun (the newest Bang Alert model, funny, because it was a silent gun) that caused the last scream of the Nouveu Fascist. And now, on his lap, the faded picture of the Neo-Nouveu Fascist, who could be the next target of the Bang Alert. Could be? Would be. Would be his next target. And afterwards, the masses would flock around him chanting revolution, the city burning and a new one emerging. Yes, would be. No going back to the man he was before the Bang Alert, the man who slept soundly but never did anything besides that. So what if hearing another last scream meant never getting rid of the nightmares. He kicked open the door of the car and stepped out, slinging the Bang Alert across his chest. Who knew what this next last scream might sound like.
written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: One Saturday morning he sat in a red car moldering in his dead uncle's garage, hidden from view, eating Lorna Doones and listening to traffic reports, justifying to God his intent to liquidate the present, more evil, more avaricious premier. Hadn't he already demonstrated superb moral consistency by personally garroting the former premier in the Department of Rhetoric's parking garage? Hadn't he, that evening, leapt into his own pit of blood and terror, and since paid the price in terms of panic attacks and nightmares, for the advancement of humanity? Would he now declare that brave killing a merely private matter by failing to publicly acknowledge his authorship and radicalize the masses to move on, killing each corrupt premier for years to come until, exhausted, he handed the torch to some fierce young protégé? Would he? Or would he turn coward and slink back to a pasty-gray anonymous existence, wherein he walked around guilty, not of a specific criminal act (for he still held his rationale sound and remembered the strangled look of terror on the premier's face with satisfaction), but of doing nothing overall, nothing yet memorable, in the direction of righteousness? Dear Lord, if at this late date he turned cowardly, wouldn't he hate himself worse than ever? Wouldn't he? And then he leaped out of the car.
written_by_MFA001.Reason: Excerpt 2 is better in terms of coherence and traces a character's interiority with more sustained attention. As opposed to the short, simple and fragmented sentences of Excerpt 1, Excerpt 2 uses more specific diction and better syntax which reflects the content. written_by_MFA005.Excerpt1: One Saturday morning, he found himself sitting in the red Arviana sportscar he’d stashed in his dead uncle’s garage. He remembered assassinating the former premier as if it were yesterday, although of course a long time had passed. For him, the intervening years had been: nightmares in the evenings, panic attacks in the mornings. Long days spent toiling in obscurity. Each year a little bit worse than the last. Meanwhile, for the new, even more evil premier? Every year he’d steadily consolidated his base. Eliminated his opponents. Misled the public. Until finally, his troubling rise to power was complete. What was a good man supposed to do? Shut the door on his uncle’s garage and continue a life of repulsive passivity – while reliving, each night, the misdeeds of his past? Or – commit to the violent path which he’d already chosen and which the present situation demanded? Kill the new premier. But this time, no more secrets, no more obscure toil. He’d claim credit right away, before he had a chance to overthink it, and declare himself the leader of a new movement of justice. He could hear, almost, his future supporters’ cheers, as he’d often heard – over and over – the thump of his car’s rear tires as they’d reversed over the former premier. He leapt from the sportscar and let the cheers carry him out into the street.

written_by_MFA021.Excerpt1: Of course, the man thought bitterly, of course the second you killed one damned autocrat a new one popped up, like an inconvenient erection, to take his place. It was Saturday. The man was sitting in a car in his dead uncle’s garage, pretending to drive. He couldn’t actually drive because he wasn’t on the run. The on the run part was over. Now he was simply in hiding. It was Saturday, and he’d killed the old premier on Tuesday, and the new premier had come to power on Thursday, and already his administration had implemented a series of performance improvement plans for striking agricultural workers that relied heavily on murder, or, as state media called it, “right-sizing the population through proactively attritionary removal policies.” The man looked down at the car. It was red. Blood red. An egregious cliché. But of course blood was red. He, of all people, should know that: his nightmares were full of it. The man stared at the steering wheel. There were two choices, right or left. Right meant he kept his head down. It wouldn’t be all bad. Right might mean a job, a house, a wife, at least once it was safe to assume a new identity. Right meant fear but not danger. His stomach turned. Left meant killing the new guy. Left meant assassination wasn’t just something he had done; “assassin” would be something he was. It would mean going public. Producing soundbites. Practicing a firm, inspirational set of his jaw for the inevitable Wanted poster. The man leaped up, determined.

written_by_MFA007.Excerpt1: I was thinking about the rubbish, the flapping plastic in the branches, the shoreline of odd boots and bottled drinks along the banks of the little stream, and for a moment my thoughts segued to the people walking towards the Lost Corner, looking for all the world like they were out for a stroll. So I stopped and waited, the wind tugging with the odd gust through my hair, and just for the frustration of it all, of how my plans had been disrupted, I imagined that all the things I had lost in life had washed up here on this spot. In front of me, on the horizon, he came trudging towards me with that odd gait he had. He was waving and laughing, as if this was a little slice of fun, and I wanted to cry out "Tommy," but I didn't, and he came on, so happy and fun, and I could feel the tears welling up. But then I reeled it back, let the fantasy unwind, and just stood in my normal stance, blinking into the wind. When I felt ready, I got in the car and went on with my life.
written_by_MFA007.Excerpt2: The wind was picking up the litter in the field. Trash bags and ripped receipts flew up and over the empty plain. I pictured my own refuse catching alongside it, everything I’d discarded coming up and toward me in the breeze. For a moment I imagined this was the place where everything I'd ever lost had washed up. A figure approached from beyond the horizon, pulled along by the gusts. It was Tommy. Or, more precisely, an image of Tommy, his left hand lifted in a wave. But I didn't let the fantasy go too far. I turned away and stopped my imagination, even as I felt the tears falling down my face -- I forced the images to disappear -- and drop back into the grass as I listened to that rush of natural force sweeping over the plain. I wasn’t crying hard or soft—in fact, after a while I wasn’t crying at all, and then I went to my car. Things couldn’t come back, I knew. They could only decompose.
written_by_MFA007.Reason: Excerpt 2 was better at conveying emotions and the unreliability of memory more effectively than Excerpt 1. Excerpt 2 does a good job of connecting the memory of Tommy to the landscape where the narrator finds themselves, and has a better flow. In Excerpt 2, the last sentence sounds like an epiphany or observation, but is written in a  nuanced way that prolongs the effect of what came before.

written_by_MFA015.Excerpt1: There once existed a time here, I suppose, when I could walk this windswept field without knocking my feet against all that came before. But now the world has filled it up with itself. Children’s playthings that were surely once my own, kites wrapped around a wayward branch, brought here as if they’d always been. But now he wasn’t anywhere, and it makes me ashamed to say I feel less of that darkness now than I did then, the day after we lost him. Tommy isn’t anywhere on the hillside. I stand only with the lesser wound and the tears that come despite it. I allow my feet to carry me back to the car, to head back into town for the night, with the hope that no one there knows my name.
written_by_MFA015.Excerpt2: I was thinking about the rubbish, the flapping plastic in the branches, the shoreline of odd boots and bottled drinks along the banks of the little stream, and for a moment my thoughts segued to the people walking towards the Lost Corner, looking for all the world like they were out for a stroll. written_by_MFA013.Excerpt2: I stood in solitude in the grass field near the beach. Ten feet away, the grass gave way to sand, which then gave way to the ocean. The wind blew, scattering rubbish and abandoned belongings. An umbrella tumbled along the shoreline, and a plastic bag drifted past me. A wide variety of objects – presumably lost at sea or lost by patrons of the beach – washed up on the shore. I imagined that anything I’d lost throughout my life could be returned to me by those waves. Then I pictured Tommy approaching from the horizon, the hair on his legs wet and flat against his skin. I saw him wave at me, and was overcome by the pain of his absence. Tears welled in my eyes. I knew that he was not really there, Tommy had long since passed. Nevertheless, I found myself longing for him to come join me in the grass. I shut my eyes and stood still for a long moment. I dried my tears and became composed. I returned to my car, without looking back. Tommy was gone, I reminded myself. Life must go on.

Meanwhile, Excerpt 2 is more general, and less interesting because of it, with lines like "The wind blew, scattering rubbish and abandoned belongings" and "I knew that he was not really there, Tommy had long since passed."

written_by_MFA001.Excerpt1: The day heated up and we heard the prayer bells in the temples, the bhangra beats from the music trucks plying their enthusiastic trade, the untuneful crying of children. It was time for coffee, and coffee, and coffee yet again, and lemon rice garnished with fried cashews, and all the other wondrous concoctions on offer in Madras. The two old men on the fourth floor of their sea-green building were released from their rooms by the day off like ships slipping their moorings, but they were rusty and they didn't go very far. Their names were blazoned across mailboxes and doorbells. Crowds of the young were descending upon Elliot's Beach, young men in cricket gear, young women deep in laughter and high fragrance, lovers hating their separation; and bikes, bikes, bikes. The sea was a water lily, the young people there were bees. Just a few short years ago Senior and Junior would have been down there too, scampering with the best, but now they had their own slow dance. They woke up just before noon and put on their two-day-old clothes. As if, by some mysterious machinery of fate, the timing wheels within their thickening, aging frames had been perfectly synchronized, they stepped out onto their verandahs at almost the same precise second and stood looking out into the world.
written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: One morning in a town quite near Chennai, the sun arose with a ferocity and began beating down on the town's residents, and there was no time to blink back dawn, the children were already awake and fussing for food, and Miss Aadhya had started on the first pot of coffee, and from her window she could hear Bollywood music, already blaring, and below her the old man whose name no one knew was praying, and above her, on the fourth floor of the Aquamarine building, Senior struggled against that veil that separates dream from reality, and broke through, and was awake. At the same time, his neighbor, Junior, awoke. The two men's eyes opened at the same time. Kabir was now calling to his friends, everyone making plans for an evening at the Elliot’s beach, the promise of cool water the only thing making it bearable to get through the hot afternoon. All the members of the town were connected to each other, as a marionette has strings attached to each of its joints, each small movement producing an equal and opposite reaction. Senior swung his legs out of bed and Junior finished brushing his teeth. The clamor of the town stirred something in both of them, and, with one elegant pull, they both lifted their heads and decided to go out, onto their own veranda.
written_by_MFA001.Reason: Excerpt 2 does a better job of handling time than Excerpt 1. It prolongs the moment before we come to Senior and Junior and their synchronized routines. Excerpt 1 employs repetition and complexity in syntax, but Excerpt 2 does a better job of handling brevity, and employing simile (as a marionette has strings attached to each of its joints) and the long sentences reflect the crowded, osmotic nature of the setting better.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: Under the heavy weight of the late afternoon sun, the city was bursting with heat, the sound of chanting prayers—Surya Mangalam, said for hope of peaceful evenings—sitar and tabla-heavy soundtracks, and children's cries rising like heat shimmers, with sweetened filter coffee laden in the air, one final push to get through to the fast-approaching dusk. But on the fourth floor of the sea-green building overlooking the blisteringly blue Indian Ocean, two elderly men, Senior and Junior, only just began their day, even as the younger generation gathered in clumps like swarms of ants, singing along to hit Tamil songs and preparing to dance and drink on Elliot's Beach once the sun set. Moving to an instinctual, silent rhythm, Senior and Junior rose as one, like two men bound by strings of fate, their walk to their verandahs as sure as the sun's journey across the sky until they sank into their chairs with the same achy movements, tilting their heads back once comfortable, two mirrors reflecting back at each other. Nothing in the world could halt this routine, their path so worn they seemed guided by more than gravity. Beneath them, a jubilant cheer rose up to greet the old men, and twin smiles stretched slowly across their faces, for they were soothed by their repetition and the companionship that repetition brings.
written_by_MFA025.Reason: The descriptions in the first excerpt veer away from cliche, brilliantly capturing both the vitality and conflict of city-life: "the untuneful crying of children," "[the old men were] released from their rooms by the day off like ships slipping their moorings, but they were rusty and they didn't go very far," "young women deep in laughter and high fragrance, lovers hating their separation." The second excerpt, however, strays toward cliche and sometimes incoherent; for example, "children's cries rising like heat shimmers," though (to my mind) heat shimmers don't visibly "rise," and the cliche "gathered in clumps like swarms of ants." The ending of the second excerpt is also overwritten, repeating the same beat: "Senior and Junior rose as one, like two men bound by strings of fate," "two mirrors reflecting back at each other," "twin smiles." In the first excerpt, the uncanny nature of this eternal coincidence is emphasized, a mystery that a reader can impose as much meaning upon as they'd like: "As if, by some mysterious machinery of fate, the timing wheels within their thickening, aging frames had been perfectly synchronized, they stepped out onto their verandahs at almost the same precise second ..."

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: Under the heavy weight of the late afternoon sun, the city was bursting with heat, the sound of chanting prayers—Surya Mangalam, said for hope of peaceful evenings—sitar and tabla-heavy soundtracks, and children's cries rising like heat shimmers, with sweetened filter coffee laden in the air, one final push to get through to the fast-approaching dusk. But on the fourth floor of the sea-green building overlooking the blisteringly blue Indian Ocean, two elderly men, Senior and Junior, only just began their day, even as the younger generation gathered in clumps like swarms of ants, singing along to hit Tamil songs and preparing to dance and drink on Elliot's Beach once the sun set. Moving to an instinctual, silent rhythm, Senior and Junior rose as one, like two men bound by strings of fate, their walk to their verandahs as sure as the sun's journey across the sky until they sank into their chairs with the same achy movements, tilting their heads back once comfortable, two mirrors reflecting back at each other. Nothing in the world could halt this routine, their path so worn they seemed guided by more than gravity. Beneath them, a jubilant cheer rose up to greet the old men, and twin smiles stretched slowly across their faces, for they were soothed by their repetition and the companionship that repetition brings.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: The day heated up and we heard the prayer bells in the temples, the bhangra beats from the music trucks plying their enthusiastic trade, the untuneful crying of children. It was time for coffee, and coffee, and coffee yet again, and lemon rice garnished with fried cashews, and all the other wondrous concoctions on offer in Madras. The two old men on the fourth floor of their sea-green building were released from their rooms by the day off like ships slipping their moorings, but they were rusty and they didn't go very far. Their names were blazoned across mailboxes and doorbells. Crowds of the young were descending upon Elliot's Beach, young men in cricket gear, young women deep in laughter and high fragrance, lovers hating their separation; and bikes, bikes, bikes. The sea was a water lily, the young people there were bees. Just a few short years ago Senior and Junior would have been down there too, scampering with the best, but now they had their own slow dance. They woke up just before noon and put on their two-day-old clothes. As if, by some mysterious machinery of fate, the timing wheels within their thickening, aging frames had been perfectly synchronized, they stepped out onto their verandahs at almost the same precise second and stood looking out into the world.
written_by_MFA025.Reason: Excerpt 2 has a more natural and compelling rhythm than Excerpt 1. The sentence "It was time for coffee, and coffee, and coffee yet again, and lemon rice garnished with fried cashews, and all the other wondrous concoctions on offer in Madras." has a nicer rhythm to it than "Under the heavy weight of the late afternoon sun, the city was bursting with heat, the sound of chanting prayers—Surya Mangalam, said for hope of peaceful evenings—sitar and tabla-heavy soundtracks, and children's cries rising like heat shimmers, with sweetened filter coffee laden in the air, one final push to get through to the fast-approaching dusk." and paints a more vivid picture of the setting and the energy of that setting.

written_by_MFA012.Excerpt1: And so the day passed. The aroma of filter coffee boiled up from the terraces of the cafes, which were filled with tourists from Tuscany, Madrid, Tyrol. The heat lingered over the city like a sinister spirit cavalry, a battalion of jinns casting spells over Elliot’s Beach; over the twin harbors and colonial promenade; over the government center and the inland districts; and back out again to one sea-green apartment building, on the fourth floor of which there were two empty verandahs. In the corresponding room, two men simultaneously awakened from their afternoon naps and stepped out onto these verandahs, which it should be said were no longer empty. Senior and Junior, as the men were called by their respective acquaintances, did not look at each other; nor did they watch the youth wander lazily from the streets to the promenade, passing marijuana cigarettes down the line like the world’s slowest relay team. Senior and Junior looked out at Elliot’s Beach, this strange sandy coin that had been cast away by fate.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: It was Saint Patrick's Day, though in her room there was no evidence of that. The world outside her window was still just ice-crusted heaps of snow and muddy patches. The sunlight reflected off them and whooshed in, bursting onto her ceiling. A tray with a small bowl of wobbly green Jell-O sat on a table over her bed, uneaten. My mother's arms lay on top of the blanket, waxy and unrecognizable to me now. I sat beside her, holding her hands, kissing them. She didn't seem to register that I was there anymore, though she was not asleep. She would not allow herself to sleep. Her eyes were wide open and still wildly, unquestionably, irrepressibly blue. Bluer than the sky. Bluer than the enamel-blue tulip-shaped pot that Bruce would get in the mail a few days later. Bluer than the water I'd swum across. Her eyes were the bluest balls of fire, and throughout those three weeks they blazed at me—bitter, bewildered, desolate, honest, true—and then the last six days, as she bore down to refuse sleep, they shifted to a blue that was so quiet, so heroically faithful, so fucking insistent. Insistent upon what, I didn't know. Her will, I supposed. To live.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: My mother died on St. Patrick’s Day. There was snow outside, and sunlight glanced off the ice and back into her hospital room. A cup of green Jell-O lingered untouched on its tray. My mother was unresponsive, but not quite asleep. Her eyes were open and vivid. There was an alertness in them still, but what she was looking at, I could not say. The bright blue of her irises was like a frozen lake, contrasting the dull wash of beige and gray shrouding the room. The sky lived inside my mother. It lived inside her then, too, even as we bided time together at the very end, knowing there was only one thing left for her to do. Her fading life was a fire flickering down to smoke—it would only last as long as there was something to burn. There was bitterness too in her eyes, then bewilderment, then a stoic, quiet heroism. A commitment to her own dignity. A promise to endure this final test, no matter how unfairly it had been imposed on her. Her eyes were so blue, my mother’s eyes, a fierce blue, a frozen lake, a sheen of ice that refused to melt, even as the sun broke it apart.
written_by_MFA029.Reason: Excerpt 1 seems makes a better choice of employing metaphors rather than similes which expresses the closeness between the narrator and the mother. Excerpt 2 has a couple of sentences that start with "there is" which makes it sound diagnostic and distant. The sentences of Excerpt 1 are more varied, and the style of including short fragments of sentences like "Bluer than the sky" etc. add to the atmosphere of the piece.

written_by_MFA009.Excerpt1: It is one thing to know something and another other thing to live it. I knew that my mother would eventually leave. All of us eventually leave. I knew that it would be hard. It was Saint Patrick’s day. I’d brought her a green cup of Jell-O, which of course she didn’t eat. When she died, I had stepped into the bathroom. I was in the shower, running water through my hair. What a ridiculous place to be when someone dies. It wasn’t that I thought there would be some movie-scene ending. That she would wait to go until I was holding her hand, looking into her eyes. That death itself would wait until I could walk her to its door and burn with her until her fire turned to smoke and her sparkling blue eyes flipped through the stages of departure. From anger to confusion to something like heroism, the whispering heroism we all embody when we face our last moment. A heroism shining in the blue of her eyes, a deep, flickering blue which proclaimed how much she wanted to stay, here, with the rest of us, even as she left. I knew, after all, that death didn’t wait for anyone. And yet, no matter how much I thought I knew, when she went, what did I find myself shouting in my head? What other than “wait”?

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: It was early winter already, and once it got dark the room was piteously cold. While there was still light, my mother got up and went into the kitchen. She filled the biggest rice bowl with water, then put it on the gas burner and waited for it to come to the boil. She snipped a length of white thread from the spool in her sewing box, and gently pressed a small pair of scissors into the steaming water. When the pain became so insupportable that she could no longer stand up, she lay down in the middle of the room. Labor began at around midnight. Trembling with fear, she used a scrap of white cloth to swaddle the newborn, as thin as a rat, and tied the thread around the barely pulsating umbilical cord. Then she severed it. She held the baby to her breast and murmured, Live, please live. Go on living and become my son. She continued to murmur to herself even as its barely open eyes closed for the final time. Go on. Keep going. After that, silence. The cold from the earthen floor invaded her back. Soaked into and through her flesh. Matching her lifeless child.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: It's strange to think of my mother as that kind of woman—the kind who bore such immense pain that she gave birth to it, all alone at the onset of the longest winter on record. The biting cold was nothing but a faint chill compared to the icy fear whispering in her ears. Was she strong enough, capable enough, to do this? Even as she boiled water to sterilize the scissors she'd use for cutting the umbilical cord, she worried the answer was a resounding no. With shaking hands, she fashioned a gown from loose fabric she kept tucked away in her sewing box. As though the faux-hospital garb could imbue the experience with a semblance of professionalism. The kind that would ward off infant death. It didn't, of course.The baby lived for a precious few moments, wheezing as my mother prayed—mindless and desperate—to a deaf god that her child should live on. Then the infant slipped away without ever uttering a cry. A silent baby, spun out of ice and glass.My mother rocked the dead baby against her chest and felt the chill of the floor creep up into the soles of her feet, freezing her into a statue of grief. Mother and baby, alone; forever.
written_by_MFA025.Reason: Excerpt 1 explains the process of a mother preparing to give birth in a more immediate fashion. Excerpt 2 on the other hand doesn't sound like a narrator engaged or familiar enough with the way events happened, often resorting to an unnatural reasoning, questioning or qualification ("Even as she boiled water to sterilize the scissors she'd use for cutting the umbilical cord, she worried the answer was a resounding no"). Excerpt 1 feels more natural because it describes, letting the emotional impact arrive on its own than hinting at it, and doesn't linger on the lifeless child for too long.

written_by_MFA011.Excerpt1: My mother once told me a story about her struggle to give birth more than forty years ago, alone in her parents’ house in Apgujeong. It was early winter. The trees were bare and the ground hard. With shaky steps, she described pacing about the kitchen while she boiled water in order to sterilize the scissors that she knew she’d need to cut the cord. With the fabric in her sewing box, she fashioned a small gown and began to wear it. During the waves of pain from her contractions, she would grip at the kitchen counter hard. Eventually after hours of this the baby came out wet and covered in a fuzzy-looking substance. Still alone, she held the newborn. Chanting a desperate plea for the little thing’s survival over and over again. But after a fleeting moment of brilliant life, her newborn child went still and died. My mother lay on the floor of the kitchen. Silently, clutching at the lifeless body of what was once vibrant inside of her. As she continued to lay there with the dead child, frozen in grief, the warmth from her body departed into the frigid floor. As though the temperature of the house were somehow reflective of her inner state.

written_by_MFA010.Excerpt1: The early days of winter remind my mother of her dead child. My father knew that my mother was due at any moment, but the roads were icy and the entire landscape had turned bare and hostile, preventing him from returning home.My mother was in labor, all by herself at home, and the ripples of her screams were absorbed by the walls, making cracks that had not existed before. In the kitchen, she tried as best as she could. She kept some water to boil in a small pot to sterilize a pair of kitchen scissors. She took off her clothes and quickly fashioned a hospital gown from some fabric that was guarded in a sewing box.Gripped by fear and pain so intense that she felt larger and more forceful than the dazzle of winter outside, my mother held a baby—slippery and blood-covered—in her arms. She had pushed and pushed, and had severed the umbilical cord with the hot pair of scissors that had burned her fingers. She chanted an old prayer, a common plea for life, but felt the warmth of the baby's body fading.My mother tells me that is when she stopped screaming. In a fleeting moment, the alchemy of the house shifted: life became death. The coldness of the floor seeped through her own body. It became impossible to tell whether the air was so still because of the cold, or her grief, or both.

written_by_MFA010.Excerpt1: It was early winter already, and once it got dark the room was piteously cold. While there was still light, my mother got up and went into the kitchen. She filled the biggest rice bowl with water, then put it on the gas burner and waited for it to come to the boil. Trembling with fear, she used a scrap of white cloth to swaddle the newborn, as thin as a rat, and tied the thread around the barely pulsating umbilical cord. Then she severed it. She held the baby to her breast and murmured, Live, please live. Go on living and become my son. She continued to murmur to herself even as its barely open eyes closed for the final time. Go on. written_by_MFA016.Excerpt1: I held the cash, folded in my hand, and my father asked the question again. Would I like to use the gift to join them for a trip to Disney World? Maybe, I said, of course I’d love to, but exams will be especially wicked this year. I don’t expect to have enough time to get away for a vacation. I looked back to my father, hoping to convey my gratitude. A piece of me did want to go. written_by_MFA016.Excerpt2: That year, at Christmas, my father gave me three crisp hundred-dollar bills instead of a gift. He invited me to join him and Chitra and Rupa and Piu at Disney World, where they were planning to spend part of the girls' winter vacation. I told him I couldn't go because school started up again the day after New Year's, but I didn't tell him that I checked the calendar first and realized that we would be back in plenty of time. To make up for it, I bought my half sisters ridiculously expensive presents—a record player for Rupa and a camera for Piu. Rupa cried when I told her I wasn't going to Disney World, which was where the record player and camera would be put to use. Piu put her arms around me. "I don't understand you, Didi," she said, still in her small, high voice. "What did we do wrong that makes you not want to go?" The truth was that in my eyes they had done nothing wrong, whereas I was punished by their mere existence. But I was still convinced that it was up to me to honor my mother's memory, just as they instinctively honored the man who was their father but not really mine. Still, I sensed that Chitra was relieved by my decision, and, by extension, so was my father.
written_by_MFA016.Reason: Excerpt 2 contains more well-crafted, subtle cues that lead to the revelation that Piu and Rupa's father is not "really" the narrator's father whereas Excerpt 1 introduces the family relationships in a more clunky, jarring way. The dialogue in Excerpt 2 sounds natural, and provides an insight into the characters' relations and ways of thinking/speaking. Excerpt 2 flows better and reads more smoothly in terms of the narrative arc of the scene.

written_by_MFA010.Excerpt2: I was home during winter. On Christmas morning, my father entered my room with a thin, white envelope in hand. Inside, there were ten twenty-dollar notes, totalling a sum of two hundred dollars, the most generous amount I had ever received from my father. I thanked him profusely, but it seemed like a prologue to the real question my father wanted to ask me. He invited me to Disney World, where he was planning to take Chitra, his new wife, and my two half-sisters, Rupa and Piu, during spring break. But I felt distant from his new family, like a string being pulled from both ends. I fabricated some excuse about having to be on-campus during that time since I was a Resident Assistant, and declined his invitation. Later that week, as we sat on the floor circled around the Christmas tree in our living room, Rupa and Piu expressed their disappointment. They could not understand why I would not want to join them in Disney World. "It's Disney World," they exclaimed. But I kept thinking of my late mother, and everything I owed her. I felt a responsibility to hold back, to stay with her memory, as if her place in our family was still untouched and unoccupied, in the same way that Rupa and Piu symbolized and remained committed to their father’s legacy. Besides, I felt, with a strange ease, that Chitra and my father, too, were relieved by my decision to leave the four of them alone to enjoy their holiday.
written_by_MFA010.Reason: The language in the second excerpt is far more stilted, formal, and overwritten ("I thanked him profusely," "I fabricated some excuse," "Rupa and Piu symbolized and remained committed to their father’s legacy"), which reads awkwardly when it's coming from a first-person narrator who seems rather young (either in high school or college). The first excerpt maintains a conversational rhythm, occasionally breaking grammatical convention, a style more appropriate for the young narrator: "invited me to join him and Chitra and Rupa and Piu," "honored the man who was their father but not really mine." The relationships between the narrator, Rupa, and Piu are also more effectively rendered in the first excerpt; in the second excerpt, the narrator describes herself as "distant from his new family, like a string being pulled from both ends" (an odd simile that doesn't quite capture a particular family dynamic), and the younger siblings "express their disappointment" when the narrator stays home. In the first excerpt, however, the narrator feels "punished by [the siblings'] mere existence," though doesn't hold it against them personally; she buys them expensive presents as an implicit apology. The children believe that they've done "something wrong" because of the narrator's distance, which the narrator regrets; these relationship dynamics are much more complex and contradictory than those expressed in the second excerpt.

written_by_MFA032.Excerpt1: Neither were presents he could have wrapped, he said, in a tone at once defensive and apologetic. “You didn’t have to get me anything,” I said. But he continued explaining, and all the while his eyes remained trained on his girls, who were prostrate under the tree. First, he conjured a creased envelope from his shirt pocket, inside which were two crisp hundred-dollar bills, but no note, no card. The invitation to Disney World came next, in that same laconic way. Unlike the cash, it was entirely intangible. Not a ticket on a red-eye to Orlando, not a room at the same overpriced hotel or a paid-for day pass—-it was simply these words: “And of course, you can join us at Disney World, if you would like.” From the kitchen, Chitra added her ringing voice to his: “Only if you want! There’s no pressure.” Meanwhile, Rupa bounded toward me and Piu followed, talking over each other as they hammered out the details.I was still holding the envelope when it struck me that the tree in their living room was new-—a real Douglas Fir, not the artificial tree, which had infused the winters of my own youth, which my mother decorated with the ornaments I made at preschool. “I would love to,” I said, looking at my father, whose eyes remained elsewhere, “but classes are starting up so soon, and with the teaching load this semester… I should work.” The girls crumpled immediately. “But, but, but why?” My father simply nodded his head gravely, as if we had come to a painful, but just, compromise. “I understand,” he said, “I understand.”

For us first-generation folk, those who came here fleeing hardship, there is always the struggle to make a home, a real home, in what remains another's land."

I truly tried to give my children roots and culture and language and traditions, but all I have succeeded in giving them is the sickness of the immigrant, the curse of the stuck-in-between. written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: When I came to the house and saw his face, I understood that his condition had worsened. He had a look of fear and incomprehension. He sat in a straight-backed chair, torpid with his medication. The lining was coming out of his jacket on both sides, into his lap. He had been forgetting where he put his papers, then losing them, too, and forgetting what he was working on. Mother would remind him: he was working on a long book about the Bible and anti-Semitism. His memory would be jogged, he would go on working until he forgot again. Father told me that day: “I am proud to have a daughter like you.” Then he added that he had nothing to say to me, nothing at all. He said, “It’s because we have isolated ourselves.” He fell silent and turned away from me. “We have isolated ourselves.” That was all. There was nothing I could say. That evening, Mother showed me a photograph taken forty years before, when my father had just got his degree: he had large brown eyes and a full head of silver hair that stood up above his head. “I can’t stand this,” she said quietly. “It is intolerable. He is such a different person.”
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: I went to see my father and found him in a much worse state than I had left him. He was disoriented and dazed, mumbling to himself about taxes and missionaries knocking on the door. He couldn't remember much about what he was working on. My mother gently reminded him that he was writing about the Bible and anti-Semitism. "Oh yes," he said, "that's right," and nodded as if to confirm this to himself. While the three of us ate supper, he turned to me and told me that he was quite proud of me. "You are a good kid," he said. "Always have been." "Is that so?" I asked. He nodded again. "I just have nothing to say to you," he said, and I told him I understood. After my mother and I washed the dishes together, she showed me a photograph from forty years ago. In it, my father had a full head of dark curls. His eyes were alert and his smile untroubled. I was perched in his lap like a small pet, staring up at him as if I had just noticed he was there. All five of my fingers could fit around his thumb. Everything that would follow in the years to come might never happen. "This was such a nice day," said my mother, stroking the photograph. "You probably don't remember, do you?" I had forgotten what her smile looked like, so I told her I remembered it perfectly.

In this case Excerpt 2 is better written than Excerpt 1. Both are coherent and fluent, but Excerpt 2 takes a more descriptive approach, which highlights the emotional impact of the scene. The ending is a perfect example.

Excerpt 1's ending is on-the-nose and explicit: “It is intolerable. He is such a different person.”

In it, the mom reflects on how much her husband has changed due to the deterioration of his mind. 

Now let's look at Excerpt 2's: "This was such a nice day," said my mother, stroking the photograph. "You probably don't remember, do you?" I had forgotten what her smile looked like, so I told her I remembered it perfectly.

In the ending of Excerpt 2, the mom and the child reminisce about a nice day together in a photo album. I couldn’t even come close to saying.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: I'm rounding off this untidy decade, meeting my deadline, and choosing to let my lovers live and unite them at the end. I want to give Robbie and Cecilia what they lost out on in life. They both died because of a simple mistake which, although it grew in significance over the years, was not difficult to expunge. Or rather, I've always known the choice was mine. Was it right, however, to let them forgive? I've no doubt my fellow criminals are either behind bars or in important salaried positions. Hypocrites—I needed their praise and confirmation, and my sisters' doubts and contempt, in order to be cured. But now I must sleep. I will close my eyes and sleep. What purpose would be served if, say, I tried to persuade my reader, by direct or indirect means, that Robbie Turner died of septicemia at Bray Dunes on June 1, 1940, or that Cecilia was killed in September of the same year by the bomb that destroyed Balham Underground station? What sense or hope or satisfaction could a reader draw from such an account? Who would want to believe that they never met again, never fulfilled their love? Who would want to believe that, except in the service of the bleakest realism? And what of that monstrous sister who systematically destroyed the love of her own sibling? I couldn't do it to them.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: I am Briony, and I am sad to report on the tragic fate of two lovers, Robbie Turner and Cecilia Tallis. Because I invented them myself, their tragedy is my own fault, but because their characters are based in reality, I cannot help but feel loyal to the truth. The fact is that Robbie and Cecilia died during World War II. Robbie succumbed to septicemia at Bray Dunes, and Cecilia perished in a bombing at Balham Underground station. Neither of them knew that I had committed a terrible wrong against them both. In my youth, I was wickedly jealous of Robbie and Cecilia and resented the affection they held for one another. Not because I desired either of them, but because I was angry and lonely and hiding in a bunker of cynicism. I was a postboy, and when Robbie went off to war, I would intercept the letters he sent to Cecelia and slide them into the rain-filled gutters. I did the same to Cecelia’s letters, and their correspondence slowly dwindled. Eventually, they stopped writing to each other altogether. I’ve been approaching this all wrong. Now is the time to let Robbie and Cecelia survive and be together, even if only in these pages. Telling the truth wouldn’t do any good, because it’s an ugly truth. I never saw Robbie and Cecelia again, their love stayed unfulfilled, and their few remaining letters are preserved only in a war museum. Maybe truth is not always better than mercy. Maybe hope survives through lies.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: The truth is much uglier than the sweet story I’ve given them. Robbie Turner and Cecilia Tallis never saw each other again, both having perished during the war. Robbie fell to septicemia at Bray Dunes, his wounds never healing right. Cecilia, my glamorous older sister, died in a bombing at the Balham Underground, dressed in the same rationed rags as any other woman. They died alone, a fault I must now agonizingly take the blame for. It was my callous childishness that ripped Robbie from Cecilia, but it is my better nature that has prompted me to write them a better ending. They find each other again, they live, and they are happy. What good would it do, I beg to know, in telling the foul truth? I’ll tell it, here and now, if only to prove my point. I never saw either of them again that year, how could I, after what I had done to Cecilia? Their love died with them, isolated and unfulfilled, with the sole evidence that they knew each other being those romantic letters preserved only in a war museum. I cannot imagine truth is worth more than the merciful fiction, but I struggle even now to know for certain if my rewrite of history is fair. I’d like to think that this hopeful conclusion, regardless of how factual it may be, holds greater value than an honest, but tragic account.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: Robbie and Cecilia were happy in my story. They faced hardships, certainly, but I conjured them, by the force of my own brittle pen, into two happy people. The world, the real world, was not as kind to them. I cannot be sure of what happened in the end, but, in all likelihood, it was this: Robbie succumbed to the brutal, unforgiving clutch of septicemia— the horror of black limbs and gasping breaths in his final moments. And dear Cecilia was decimated by a bomb at Balham Underground station. Is it selfishness, then, or a mercy, this ending I’ve given them, this happiness? In my tale, there is no sickness traveling through the veins, no limbs blown off. There is only contentment and love, a warm and certain kind. Why tell the truth, when it is something almost unspeakably miserable? The truth: that I never saw them again, after what happened. That I could not face my sister. That their letters—tender and sorrowful —are preserved only in a war museum, words of desperate longing fossilized behind panes of glass. It’s this business of truth I continue to return to—always this business of truth. Is the truth better than what I have done? Have I committed an act of cowardice, in my story, or an act of love? For I loved them both; still, I do. And I gave them mercy, a happy ending, perhaps more meaningful than the tragic nature of their lives. I gave them each other.

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: At one time I imagined that being a desirable woman made you an object and being an undesirable woman made you a person. In the years since I’ve learned that being an undesirable woman actually makes you less than a person, makes you something subhuman. If you are a woman but not a beautiful woman, are instead a fat woman scorned by men and more largely scorned by a society that understands women as objects subjected to male desire, then you are not allowed to be human. And this is me. Not quite a human because of the body I live in. written_by_MFA002.Excerpt1: To be a feminist — perhaps, to be a woman at all — is to teeter on the edge of a chasm between principle and performance. This week I rode the subway for the first time in months. In a moment of hyperperception, I swept my awareness over the scene: dusty bottles at the edge of the track, a lone rat scurrying into the bowels of the public transit system, three men hulking at one side of a gum-stained bench, blasting Drake on a tinny speaker. I found myself acutely aware not only of my perception of the scene, but of the men’s perception of my perception of the scene, and my perception of the men’s perception of my perception. Was I to admonish these men for listening to an artist well-known for wrapping misogyny in a catchy tune and feeding it to vulnerable audiences of young, troubled men? Did they expect this of me —were they waiting for my reprimand, already preparing their rebuttal? Should I be bracing myself for a flurry of calm downs and lighten ups? I did none of these things. Instead I found myself nodding slightly to the beat. Because, to tell the truth — it was a catchy tune. Perhaps this makes me a bad feminist. Perhaps I am a bad feminist for wearing pink flowy maxi dresses that highlight my femininity, a choice in line with the beauty standards and fashion requirements long used to subjugate women — to make women seem weaker, more delicate, more frivolous. Perhaps I am a bad feminist for ceding, at times, to this perception of the feminine as frail and foolish when it conveniences me: allowing a gallant male stranger to change my tire on the side of the road or letting my professional persona slip in a rare moment of vulnerability. Perhaps I am a bad feminist for thinking any of this at all — by discounting my true nature, I am participating in the classic erasure of women’s personal desires in favor of the welfare of others. Perhaps I am a bad feminist. But I am also a tired feminist. Where does it end? Am I to be trapped forever in this infinite moral calculation of every action and every thought? Candidly, I don’t mind being a bad feminist, if it means I can be like the subway rat — revolting and dirty, maybe, but free to scurry at my whim.

written_by_MFA001.Excerpt1: I often long to be a better feminist. I know what a good feminist, a correct feminist, looks like. A woman who shouts down men who try to dominate her, a woman who refuses to ever be under the thumb of a man and shows up at all the right marches and always has her pink pussy hat at the ready for whatever protests comes next. I see those women, and I respect them, and often, I want to be them. But the fact of the matter is sometimes when men try to dominate me I let them, so they can mow my lawn without much of a fuss. When my father rattles off five misogynistic things in a row on our phone call I am silent, because I am too tired to fight back. And sometimes it is too cold outside to protest, pink pussy hat or no pink pussy hat. I want to be a good feminist, one that believes that women can do anything by themselves and we don't need any man. But sometimes I long to be cared for, sometimes I think I really do need a man. I long to be soft and weepy, and wear long flowing dresses and lipstick. This is the type of women the patriarchy praises, and feminists despise - and sometimes that is the type of woman I want to be. I want to be a good feminist, but often I am a bad feminist. I like dancing to rap songs with lyrics that are categorically misogynistic. I like wearing pink and scrolling through Pinterest pictures of those 'perfect' women that I know are there to make all us regular women feel terrible about ourselves. I like wearing those long maxi dresses that make me look like I could be on a farm, tending chickens and popping out babies dutifully for my husband. written_by_MFA011.Excerpt1: You know, he says, it’s going to be really hard for me to be apart from you, Marianne. Like, I literally don’t think I would have had the life I’ve had without you. Marianne smiles and looks down at the floor, where a puddle of water has formed from the snow in an obscure shape. She thinks about the first night she met Connell, the kiss they shared atop the washing machine in his mother’s house, and says, My life obviously wouldn’t be the same, either. You’ve done so much for me, really. When we first met, that first night at the house, I felt like I wasn’t worth anything to anyone. To be honest, there were nights when I might’ve wished I was dead. But you saw me, and you changed the way I saw myself. You’ve given me something that I didn’t even know was possible. Connell chuckles and wipes away with his shirtsleeve at a tear that has formed at the corner of his eye. I’m not sure I would know what it’s like to be seen without you, she continues. We’re sort of like two plants that have shared the same soil for their whole lives, always growing around each other without realizing it. But even though we’ve done so much good for each other, I know that things change and that we can’t control what will happen in the future. As she speaks, Marianne knows that things may never be the same between herself and Connell. She remembers again that first night in the house and the feeling of his warm lips on her ear, then imagines coming home to an empty house each night, with no one to leave empty mugs of tea out drying on the big windowsill overlooking the park. To be without him is almost unimaginable; then again, loneliness, she thinks, is a small price to pay for Connell’s happiness.
written_by_MFA011.Excerpt2: Marianne says nothing for a time. Her arm, his arm, her leg. Maybe we could, if it’s just going to be a year, she says. Don’t think other people have gone through life without having long periods of time on their own, you know. Yes, he says. I just love you so much. I know, she says. I love you too. He nods, breathing in. Her large dark eyes are like openings to something. Without you I would be nothing, he says. I would just be a shadow walking around the town. I saw you, I really saw you. I wanted you to exist here and be happy. Anyway, he says. I believe we have done a lot of good for each other. Yes. I know. It’s sad because it was the happiest time of her life, and it’s over now. Never again will she have what she had then, the love and care of another person. Never again will they be two plants sharing the same soil, one leaning in the light, the other languishing in the shade. She doesn’t blame him, she no longer believes her unhappiness is inevitable. No one can be what another person wants them to be. But she adds: You should go, if you want to. I’ll always be here. You know that. Does she think it’s possible to belong to someone this way? So concretely, so unquestionably. To have someone belong to you. The scene could still unite them, for those minutes, so that it would be unthinkable to be separated from him again, unthinkable that they had wasted so long already. But she knows he won’t be confused about what he has to do with his life. She knows he’ll go and she’ll stay, and that’s how it will be. People can really change one another. You should go, she says. I’ll always be here.

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt2: Remember how different we were when we first met, Connell said. Marianne paused, face warmed by his shoulder. She thought that perhaps they were at the sort of height one jumps from and survives jumping from, that she would, despite the loneliness, be able to carry on from this: two plants sharing a large pot, space and light made for them both as their stems grew in opposite directions. Often she felt this way with her friends. Sometimes young friendships to her seemed featherweight and passing, and even in the depths of real connection, these relationships felt unimportant and survivable. Survivable, she meant, if they ended. But with Connell, she would not really survive losing him forever. Marianne could not imagine for them any real or permanent parting, nothing as serious as death. This moment between them was unlike that unfathomable permanence and unlike how she felt with friends, and bearable for it. She told him this.You've been the person who shaped my life, really, Connell said, who I am today. She shrugged against him and felt sick to imagine them parted but could see in that possibility an uncertain future that took nothing from their certain past. You were the first person to really see me, she said, and then laughed at herself, insecure. In this way, pieces of their early dynamic still clung to her: a certain unsteadiness that sometimes made her mean but never cruel. A feeling, perhaps, that despite all they had meant to each other, there was some part of her still unworthy and always seeking more of him. But Connell smoothed her hair and sighed, his inhaling chest elevating hers, and said sadly, We were made to make each other into adults, I think. For a moment they, attached to each other, shared breath in an afternoon marked by parting but not only by sadness.

written_by_MFA001.Excerpt1: I’m ready now, my friend said, and I said nothing because I didn't know what to say. There were ways people did these sorts of things, she explained to me, certain drugs people used. But she couldn't tell me which drugs. For my protection. Protection against what?, I wondered, but I didn't ask her. That seemed wrong to say. I wanted to ask her about when she was planning on taking these drugs, exactly, but I worried that line of questioning was unthinkable, morbid. I didn't want it to seem like I wanted a date so I could put it on my calendar and plan around it. Already, though, I was thinking about my plans. The mail stacking in the mailbox with each day I stayed with my friend. You don't have to tell me anything you don't want to, I said -- and then I worried that made it sound like I didn't really want to hear anything at all. But she just said, this way it's all in my hands. Her hands: frail, slightly shaking. She was ready to die, she told me, she wanted to get it over with, it felt like that was the way her body was heading. All the ups and downs with the treatments just delaying the inevitable. She was bound to die, just like the coming of the Lord was bound to happen, she said. She glanced upwards and my eyes followed hers. Nothing and no one appeared, and she looked back at me. Just promise you won't tell anyone, she said. I won't, I said -- it was a lie. The weight of the secret was too great. Her plans were too great, too serious. I didn't know what to do. I had already told someone else.
written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: Look. I've been the one making the plan, and I want to be the one to execute it. There was a silence before she spoke again. I'll be honest, I'm not the kind of person who's so crazy about living that I want to put off dying as long as I possibly can. I'll be ready. In fact, I'm already impatient. But like I told you, no one can be sure how the cancer's going to behave. We all know there are sometimes surprises, and the body can be very stubborn about giving up, and it's always possible that treatment might be delayed. And I want this as natural as possible. I want to be in a certain state. I don't want to be in distress. I don't want to be rescued. I don't want my hand held. I'm sorry, but I just can't commit to any particular moment, any particular day. It could happen tomorrow. It could happen in a couple of weeks. As the saying goes, it'll be like the coming of the Lord. You won't know the day or the hour. But don't worry, she added, feeling the words catch in her throat. You'll know the minute afterward. Remembering my full mailbox, I said I'd want my mail held if I went away for a week or more. She pressed her lips together and frowned. I had gone too far. The truth was, it was unthinkable for me to bring all this up at all. I'd rather you didn't mention the drug, or how I got it, to anyone. You understand, don't you? For your own protection—and for mine. But this promise I had already broken. I had already shared this information with someone.
written_by_MFA001.Reason: The short, clipped sentences of Excerpt 1 create a strong sense of anxiety and guilt that prepares the reader for the revelation at the end of the excerpt, that the narrator has told someone their friend intends to commit suicide. For example, "For my protection. Protection against what?, I wondered, but I didn't ask her. That seemed wrong to say," generates a jittery energy, with the tight beats of each fragment building on each other to suggest the narrator's discomfort and general stress about the situation. Running throughout the whole excerpt is the narrator's repetition of the idea that her friend's death is inevitable, with lines like, "She was ready to die" and "she was bound to die" creating an almost mantra-like quality. This likewise helps build a sense of tension. Excerpt 2, by contrast, is almost entirely the friend's monologue to the narrator, so there is very little of the narrator's internal reactions. There is a cool, almost callous comment from the narrator immediately after the conclusion of the monologue: "I said I'd want my mail held if I went away for a week or more," then a jarringly earnest internal confession, "The truth was, it was unthinkable for me to bring all this up at all," and it's so jarring because before the narrator mentally admits to the having told someone, this is the only moment of interiority. It's not a shock when the Excerpt 2 narrator reveals they have told someone about the friend's intention to commit suicide because we haven't seen the narrator's internal reaction to the knowledge.

written_by_MFA007.Excerpt1: I was on my way to see the woman as a visitor, riding up in an elevator filled with doctors and nurses clutching clipboards, and patients doubled over in pain. "Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine is needed in the consulting room," an announcement came over the PA system. Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine, however, never showed his face.My purpose in visiting her was clear enough: I intended to meet with her, regain her trust, and convince her to let me see the bag put to its intended use one last time."Would you mind undoing the ends of the cord so I can check how you attached it?" "Would you like me to take a photograph of you wearing it?" "Do you need to have another hole punched in the strap to make it longer?" I rehearsed these lines in my head. I realized I had never spoken to her so politely.In truth, I simply needed to make her put the bag down for a moment. I planned to face her, extend to her all the gratitude I felt for having been allowed to sew the bag on. Then, once she let her guard down, I would press the shears to her chest. The shears were hidden, but soon she'd feel the cold steel pressed against her belly, slowly moving up toward her breasts. She'd moan in fear. I'd then carefully—oh so carefully—slice through the flesh as though cutting through layers of delicate silk. When the final thread had been cut and the heart was liberated from her chest, there would be no need anymore to smile and exchange pleasantries. The bag would be mine alone. But not because I wanted it. No, I was doing this to restore the proper order of things. I'd hold the bag in one hand and the shears in the other. The elevator finally climbed to the sixth floor.
written_by_MFA007.Excerpt2: The elevator opened onto the third floor, and I flattened myself against the side as a patient and his doctor exited. “Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine,” said the intercom. On the fourth floor, two nurses entered the crowded elevator. As I was forced into the corner, I heard “Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine” bleat over the intercom again. I had two more floors left before I’d reach hers. Whether Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine appeared or not, I had a plan, infallible and precise. I would see her, lying prone on her hospital bed, and hold up the bag. “I have to apologize for everything,” I’d say. “I made this bag for you. I crafted it myself.”“How lovely,” she’d respond, her voice lax from the painkillers. “How many pockets does it have?”“Six,” I’d say. “What material did you use to stitch it together?” “Cowhide. It feels like a baby’s cheek. Feel it,” I’d say. “Please, feel it.”When she reached out to touch her finger on the belly of the bag, I’d lean over and, taking my shears out, throw away the hospital linens covering her body. Then, as her hand caressed the bag’s soft skin, I’d cut into her chest. I’d trim the strings of the heart first, the extraneous vessels and tissue that fastened it to her insides. Once it was freed, I’d toss the shears aside. Then I’d grasp it with my bare hand. In my palm, her heart would fit like a baseball. After it was done, I’d leave, my bag in hand, alone. “Dr Y. from Respiratory Medicine,” repeated the intercom. As another nurse shuffled past me, I clutched the bag to my chest. Its delicate construction couldn’t dull the shears hidden inside. Their blades were so sharp that, when the elevator moved upward once more, they pricked me. The elevator dinged for the sixth floor.

Excerpt 2, on the other hand, layers plot and character details in a way that widens the interpretation of the narrator's attributes and their relationship to the woman: "I wondered if she'd notice the care I put into making her bag the same way I noticed the care with which she used to tend her shrubs...I had seen her work, but she had never seen mine." This delicate back-and-forth between their genuine interest/admiration and their unsettling voyeurism feels better scaffolded, and more climactic by the passage's ending.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: Like most people, Walter and Patty Berglund had a past life. Unlike most people, this past life took place in St. Paul, Minnesota. In the Berglunds’ current life in Washington D.C., where they had moved two years prior, Walter was falling from grace. It was perhaps less like a fall and more like a plummet. An article in the New York Times had just been published, ruthlessly exposing his corrupt dealings with the coal industry. These misdeeds included but were not limited to bribery, extortion, embezzlement, and profiteering. In describing Walter, the article made generous use of words like “arrogant” and “ethically compromised,” which Walter’s old neighbors in Ramsey Hill found difficult to process. In their memories, he had been an idealistic, environmentally conscious man who commuted across town by bike even in the most vicious of sleet and hail. Many had once considered Walter to be the embodiment of rural, green values—someone who set an aspirational standard for the rest to follow. It seemed he had experienced a change of heart since leaving town. When the Berglunds first moved to Ramsey Hill, they worked doggedly to revitalize the neglected neighborhood. When asked what brought them to Ramsey Hill, the Berglunds gave vague half-answers about the real estate market and wanting to be involved in something from the ground floor. They bought a cheap, shambling Victorian house and renovated it with stoic resolve. Together, they slowly won out over every obstacle they faced, from vandalism to unruly neighbors to general disrepair. Patty, a former athlete, always liked a challenge. She wheeled her infant son’s stroller through the gritty neighborhood, weaving deftly between cracks in the sidewalk, never breaking her strong, assured pace. She marched through a regiment of cooking, cleaning, repairing, and caring for the baby with an endurance forged in years of grueling, all-day swim practices. Even her indulgences—public radio and zinfandel—were stringently measured, slotted into the schedule with militant rigidity. Walter and Patty gave every indication that they were here in Ramsey Hill to stay, and nobody thought otherwise. But as the Berglunds built up their house and the surrounding area, they were really building less of a home and more of a ladder.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: Like most people, Walter and Patty Berglund had a past life. Unlike most people, this past life took place in St. Paul, Minnesota. In the Berglunds’ current life in Washington D.C., where they had moved two years prior, Walter was falling from grace. It was perhaps less like a fall and more like a plummet. An article in the New York Times had just been published, ruthlessly exposing his corrupt dealings with the coal industry. These misdeeds included but were not limited to bribery, extortion, embezzlement, and profiteering. In describing Walter, the article made generous use of words like “arrogant” and “ethically compromised,” which Walter’s old neighbors in Ramsey Hill found difficult to process. In their memories, he had been an idealistic, environmentally conscious man who commuted across town by bike even in the most vicious of sleet and hail. Many had once considered Walter to be the embodiment of rural, green values—someone who set an aspirational standard for the rest to follow. It seemed he had experienced a change of heart since leaving town. When the Berglunds first moved to Ramsey Hill, they worked doggedly to revitalize the neglected neighborhood. When asked what brought them to Ramsey Hill, the Berglunds gave vague half-answers about the real estate market and wanting to be involved in something from the ground floor. They bought a cheap, shambling Victorian house and renovated it with stoic resolve. Together, they slowly won out over every obstacle they faced, from vandalism to unruly neighbors to general disrepair. Patty, a former athlete, always liked a challenge. She wheeled her infant son’s stroller through the gritty neighborhood, weaving deftly between cracks in the sidewalk, never breaking her strong, assured pace. She marched through a regiment of cooking, cleaning, repairing, and caring for the baby with an endurance forged in years of grueling, all-day swim practices. Even her indulgences—public radio and zinfandel—were stringently measured, slotted into the schedule with militant rigidity. Walter and Patty gave every indication that they were here in Ramsey Hill to stay, and nobody thought otherwise. But as the Berglunds built up their house and the surrounding area, they were really building less of a home and more of a ladder.

written_by_MFA007.Excerpt1: In St. Paul — or, at the very least, in the Ramsey Hill neighborhood — Walter and Patty Berglund were remembered as decent folks, despite the fact that they’d moved to Washington, D.C. two years ago. The Walter Berglund of the New York Times article, the “arrogant” and “ethically compromised” Walter, sounded like a different entity entirely, an evil twin or the result of a personality-altering traumatic brain injury. When he lived in Ramsey Hill, Walter would commute to work on his bike because it reduced carbon emissions, never mind the below-zero winters or the bluffs after Summit Avenue. During city council meetings, he gave passionate speeches about sorting plastics from paper. The Walter of Ramsey Hill believed in a better America, a green America, wild in its terrain, a patchwork of sustainable farms. Now the news, or at least the decent people at The New York Times and The Associated Press and The Washington Post, too, accused him of taking bribes from the coal industry. Walter and Petty first moved to Ramsey Hill back when it was still a neglected neighborhood; they thought of themselves as pioneers, do-gooders who could be the first to clean it up. With the little money they had, they’d bought a run-down Victorian house, and through the following years, they poured everything into that house’s restoration, fighting off plumbing failures, electrical outages, a neighbor with a penchant for yelling at his wife on the street, rotted wood, basement floods, and teen vandals — to address the latter, Patty had used a bat and a few stern, almost maternal, words. Patty, a former cheerleader for UMN, never fit into the neighborhood, visually speaking, though it hardly seemed to bother her. In the mornings, she jogged with her stroller, her blonde ponytail swinging behind her as she swerved to avoid the sidewalk feces, her face unflinching as the occasional truck driver whistled at her. In the afternoons, she painted the sidings of the house or installed kitchen tile between diaper changes and nursing sessions. In the evenings, she sat on the couch after preparing dinner, sipping a glass of zinfandel and listening to NPR, a radio station that would, in the unforeseeable future, refer to her as “the wife of disgraced politician, Walter Berglund.”
