written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: Ifemelu looks at her Frenchwoman host and her American husband, both grinning with rows of straight teeth, and puts down her wine glass. The wine loosens her tongue and she cannot help it when she says, "America is obsessed with race. I never realized how much until I moved here and now I can't get away from it." She speaks quickly, the words coming easily to her despite the many eyes now firmly fixed on her. With her captive audience, she could almost be a college professor, the kind that reminds her of cult leaders. The watching usually makes her skin crawl, but now it feels like the eyes are attached to ears that are earnestly listening. She tells them that every time she goes outside, she is acutely aware of her blackness in a way she has never experienced before. "Because I'm so aware," she says, "I'm extra-aware when I'm with a boyfriend. And it's not just me, it's everyone in an interracial relationship! You don't want your boyfriend accusing you of being too sensitive, you know? Men always call women crybabies, so you don't want him thinking you're any more emotional than he already believes. Confirmation bias! So you pretend it doesn't bother you, even though it really does. And you can't complain to anyone else about your white boyfriend, either, because there's always some old crone muttering about how, well," she pitches her voice for a biting mimicry. "Interracial relationships used to be illegal, which is so infantilizing to point out! Just because things used to be worse, doesn't mean I can't be frustrated by them still being bad!" she says, and she looks at her nice, liberal audience, and how they've all put down their forks as if eating would mean they aren't listening. They're leaning forward, watching her like a specimen under a microscope. Her hosts are chuckling to each other, but nodding along. Next to them, the poet, who has been a far quieter guest than Ifemelu, tugs at the Frenchwoman's sleeve to nervously compliment one of the side dishes. She absently thanks him and gestures for Ifemelu to keep going. Blaine's face is shuttered, and Ifemelu takes another sip of wine. Distantly, she thinks she might regret this tomorrow. She opens her mouth, though, and says, "It was like that with my ex-boyfriend, Curt." Blaine's lip twitches. Ifemelu says, "He just couldn't understand."
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: "Race doesn't really exist for you because it has never been a barrier. Black folks don't have that choice. Like, growing up in Nigeria, I knew I was black, but I didn't really think about it until I came to America. Then I came here and—God, it hits you immediately. Race becomes everything. You can't say in good faith race doesn't matter when you are dating a white man. The minute you step outside, things are apparent. When somebody walks into a bar that you are sitting in with your white husband, they don't see a man and a woman; they see a white man and a black woman. It doesn't matter what they say. At the grocery store, they'll ask you, separately, if you need help, because, of course, it's such a stretch to imagine that you're together. And you are thinking about that, you are aware of that, but your white partner is not thinking about it in the same way. Or he is not thinking about it at all.So you stifle your feelings because you don't want him to dismiss you by saying you're being paranoid, or remind you that, hey, until the sixties, you all wouldn't even have been able to date, so at least you're doing good. And of course if you say any of this to your nice liberal American friends, they say, 'But we're not like that.' You see, in America's public discourse, 'but' is usually a prelude to rationalization. And when you say, 'but we're not like that' to black people, what you're also saying is that you're refusing to acknowledge the truth of their experience."The host, a Frenchwoman who lived with her American husband, looked amused, as though enjoying the possibility that discord was coming.The poet appeared uncomfortable, eager to suggest a safer topic. "Darling, should I save the onion dip?" she asked the host.The other guests were all watching as though they had never imagined they would feel this way: enjoined in intellectual discomfort by a person they had thought was intellectually like them. Ifemelu was emboldened by the white wine. A part of her wanted to apologize for not playing to the right audience, but a part of her knew she would do it all again.Perhaps she had gone too far, but she was plugged in now, the center of their attention. Even Blaine's expression was unreadable; she could not tell what he was thinking. She took another sip of wine. "So, my ex-boyfriend Curt was the first white man I dated."
written_by_MFA025.Reason: I prefer the coherence and fluency in E2--it's focus on dialogue at the beginning, without getting bogged down in details about the host and the boyfriend until those initial ideas about race and Ifemlu's relationship have been established, make it much more easy to follow. E1 also has some issues with clarity and originality ("Blaine's face is shuttered" and "like a specimen under a microscope) and the phrase "biting mimicry" that interrupts the dialogue is distracting and awkward.

written_by_MFA001.Excerpt1: "It means something different, to be Black here. Something wide and heavy, and I wasn't expecting that, when I moved. You can meet someone, and they can seem perfect for you. But if they're white - when you go outside, that's all anyone cares about. Their whiteness, your Blackness. And you have to dodge the dirty looks people give you on the street. And if you want to talk about that, with your partner - suddenly you're the bad guy. You can't bring up how racism makes you feel because all of a sudden they're defensive and angry, they think you're calling them a racist. And they can't understand, really, what it feels like to be looked at the way people sometimes look at me. Like I'm nothing, or less than nothing." As Ifemelu spoke, Blaine's lips were pressing into a thin, straight line. He looked studiously at his fork, refusing to meet her eyes. A part of her brain cautioned her to stop talking, but the wine had made her tongue heavy and her jaw loose. "People are always saying to me - fifty years ago, you would have been locked up if you tried to date a white man, look at how far this country has come! That's all people ever want to talk about, how much progress has been made. Everyone expects me to be so grateful and happy to be here, but all I can think about is how awful it feels sometimes, to live here and always be thinking about how other people are seeing me." Ifemelu paused. Her own words were echoing in her ears, and she felt the stinging truth of them. The poet seized upon this break and pointed down at his plate. "How did you make these Brussels sprouts?" he said, and the French host seemed not to hear him at all; her eyes were trained on Ifemelu. "But why so pessimistic?" she asked, almost breathlessly, leaning in like Ifemelu was delivering scandalous gossip. "Maybe the people in your past were just wrong for you in some way. Maybe they're skewing your perception." Ifemelu drained the rest of her glass and tightened her fingers around the stem. "The people in my past didn't skew my perception - they showed me the truth," Ifemelu said bitterly. "Let me tell you about this one man I used to date - his name was Curt."

written_by_MFA015.Excerpt1: How this went was, you go about your post-cheating days with your bad-ass  from Salcedo, unworried about what you’d done, how you’d done it, who you’d done it with, and for a good long while the two of you are what you might call happy. written_by_MFA002.Excerpt1: My awkward undergraduate years are better left undiscussed, but lately I have found myself turning them over in my head in search of an insight that has eluded me since – what drove me to join my university’s chapter of the Black Panther Party? Ostensibly I supported the movement and its ideologies, but in retrospect – and in all honesty – my desire to resist the oppression of my people was, perhaps, not the most pertinent factor in my decision. Really I joined the Party as a means of proving myself – more specifically, proving my Blackness. And to whom was this posturing directed? Certainly at the white and Black basketball players alike who laughed me off the court when I mumbled “Egads” upon a fumbled shot. Certainly at Todd Henderson, the literary critic who called my retelling of Aeschylus’s Prometheus Bound “disconcertingly cerebral” for an author like me. And candidly, perhaps at myself. I needed to convince myself that I was Black enough. And maybe I still do, decades later. The other day I attended a literary party in the city and somehow found myself sucked into a conversation with an agent of an acquaintance. “Don’t bother with the Achilles,” the agent told me. (Privately I considered correcting his pronunciation of Aeschylus, then decided it wasn’t worth the effort.) “It’s not what they want. They’re looking for true, gritty, real stories of Black life. They want authenticity.” This puzzled me. I asked him to define authentic. What makes me, a Black man writing material guided by my lived experience, not authentically Black? To this, the agent laughed, clapped me on the shoulder, and moved on to debate the prevalence of body shaming in social media with a bemused performance artist perusing the hors d’oeuvres. Today, as I write, I consider my opinion on it all – Blackness, whiteness, authenticity. I don’t really believe in race. I regard race as a construct of convenience, a societal demarcation on which I rarely dwell. And yet, I recognize the self-indulgent folly in the popular adage, I don’t see color. I am not blind to the concrete consequences of racial divides: oppression, discrimination, violence, subjugation. But there’s something artificial and contrived about the Blackness that I feel I must actively demonstrate.
written_by_MFA002.Excerpt2: When I was in college I joined the Black Panther Party. I wore a black turtleneck sweater and black beret and stood outside in the cold with arms full of old newspapers. I wasn’t trying to prove my ideological stance. I was trying to prove that I was indeed Black. It seems that no one, Black or white, thought I was Black enough. Once when a loose ball was bounding about on a basketball court, I muttered “Egads,” and people’s heads turned. When I savored a biscuit and described it as sublime, I received odd looks. And, of course, I was not nearly gloomy or angry enough as a writer. Of a retelling of Aeschylus, a reviewer wrote: “The novel has some merit, but do we really need this from a Black man?” A literary agent puffed up with plastic pride told me at a New York party that nobody wanted an intellectual Black man, especially one doing retellings of Greek plays. I pointed out that I actually knew Greek. He laughed and asked if that was a joke and suggested I should write some true, gritty real stories of Black life instead. He glanced across the room at a woman with strings of beads in her otherwise naked Afro, then turned back to me. He said if I gave him a story about cocaine and drive-bys and baby mamas and regrets, he would make me a millionaire. I told him to fuck off and that my life was Black and that the stories I wrote were in fact Black stories. I was sure that he had no idea what I was talking about.He sniffed at the air, feigned boredom and proceeded to chat up the Afro woman, who I heard later was a performance artist. I knew I was Black, saw myself as Black, but race was a fiction. A handy one, a stupid one, a dangerous one, but a fiction nonetheless. To be honest I don’t think about race much, except when my liberal guilt compels me to consider it or when I read about some thirteen-year-old kid being shot by some cop, and then I remember that though race is a construct without a basis in the natural world, those bullets are quite real and deadly.
written_by_MFA002.Reason: E1 is more coherent and compelling than E2. written_by_MFA002.Excerpt1: My awkward undergraduate years are better left undiscussed, but lately I have found myself turning them over in my head in search of an insight that has eluded me since – what drove me to join my university’s chapter of the Black Panther Party? Ostensibly I supported the movement and its ideologies, but in retrospect – and in all honesty – my desire to resist the oppression of my people was, perhaps, not the most pertinent factor in my decision. Really I joined the Party as a means of proving myself – more specifically, proving my Blackness. And to whom was this posturing directed? Certainly at the white and Black basketball players alike who laughed me off the court when I mumbled “Egads” upon a fumbled shot. Certainly at Todd Henderson, the literary critic who called my retelling of Aeschylus’s Prometheus Bound “disconcertingly cerebral” for an author like me. And candidly, perhaps at myself. I needed to convince myself that I was Black enough. And maybe I still do, decades later. The other day I attended a literary party in the city and somehow found myself sucked into a conversation with an agent of an acquaintance. “Don’t bother with the Achilles,” the agent told me. (Privately I considered correcting his pronunciation of Aeschylus, then decided it wasn’t worth the effort.) “It’s not what they want. They’re looking for true, gritty, real stories of Black life. They want authenticity.” This puzzled me. I asked him to define authentic. What makes me, a Black man writing material guided by my lived experience, not authentically Black? To this, the agent laughed, clapped me on the shoulder, and moved on to debate the prevalence of body shaming in social media with a bemused performance artist perusing the hors d’oeuvres. Today, as I write, I consider my opinion on it all – Blackness, whiteness, authenticity. I don’t really believe in race. I regard race as a construct of convenience, a societal demarcation on which I rarely dwell. And yet, I recognize the self-indulgent folly in the popular adage, I don’t see color. I am not blind to the concrete consequences of racial divides: oppression, discrimination, violence, subjugation. But there’s something artificial and contrived about the Blackness that I feel I must actively demonstrate.
written_by_MFA002.Excerpt2: When I was in college I joined the Black Panther Party. I wore a black turtleneck sweater and black beret and stood outside in the cold with arms full of old newspapers. I wasn’t trying to prove my ideological stance. I was trying to prove that I was indeed Black. It seems that no one, Black or white, thought I was Black enough. Once when a loose ball was bounding about on a basketball court, I muttered “Egads,” and people’s heads turned. When I savored a biscuit and described it as sublime, I received odd looks. And, of course, I was not nearly gloomy or angry enough as a writer. Of a retelling of Aeschylus, a reviewer wrote: “The novel has some merit, but do we really need this from a Black man?” A literary agent puffed up with plastic pride told me at a New York party that nobody wanted an intellectual Black man, especially one doing retellings of Greek plays. I pointed out that I actually knew Greek. He laughed and asked if that was a joke and suggested I should write some true, gritty real stories of Black life instead. He glanced across the room at a woman with strings of beads in her otherwise naked Afro, then turned back to me. He said if I gave him a story about cocaine and drive-bys and baby mamas and regrets, he would make me a millionaire. I told him to fuck off and that my life was Black and that the stories I wrote were in fact Black stories. I was sure that he had no idea what I was talking about.He sniffed at the air, feigned boredom and proceeded to chat up the Afro woman, who I heard later was a performance artist. I knew I was Black, saw myself as Black, but race was a fiction. A handy one, a stupid one, a dangerous one, but a fiction nonetheless. To be honest I don’t think about race much, except when my liberal guilt compels me to consider it or when I read about some thirteen-year-old kid being shot by some cop, and then I remember that though race is a construct without a basis in the natural world, those bullets are quite real and deadly.

written_by_MFA030.Excerpt1: I remember those college days. The grass peeking over cement, the columns of the buildings thick, stuffed, presumably, with knowledge. Though, admittedly, I had a hard time juggling it all, having joined the Panthers on campus, less for their social cause, and more to reject the budding questions about my Blackness. Needless to say, it didn't work. Everywhere I went, strangers, white and Black, would tell me I wasn't Black enough. The white friends wanted to know why I didn't keep a gun, like a real Black Panther, and the Panthers wanted to know why I was so busy doing the white man's homework. Once, an entire basketball court stopped the game to laugh for five minutes when they heard me mutter egads after missing a shot. I can take these teases in everyday life, but when it comes to my literature, that's when the blade cuts deepest. The most recent was a slack-mouthed reviewer who wondered why my last novel, a retelling of Aeschylus, did not portray adequately, as they put it, "the Black man's experience." This was no unusual comment. At a literary party, I was once told to abandon my passion for classic retellings in favor of "true, gritty real stories of Black life." There were millions to be made here, an agent had said. When I refused their suggestion, telling them that all of my stories are stories of Black life, because I, a Black life, made them, they moseyed over to a performance artist, with whom they spent the rest of the evening talking about sword-swallowing. I looked at the paintings on the walls of the luxury Harlem apartment, all of Black strife, contorted faces, hands in yearning, bodies that seldom looked like bodies. Pictures of poverty worth millions. I couldn't say that I believed in race at all - I saw it merely as a construct. And yet, its grasp over me and those around me felt crushing, inevitable, real. I knew if I burned the apartment to the ground, as I felt the growing desire to do, the newspaper would not say "Established Author Sets Party Ablaze in Fit of Misplaced Justice." No, it would simply say, "Black Man Commits Arson." That would be how I would be remembered.

written_by_MFA015.Excerpt1: There came a point in my life when I seemed to have to "prove" my Blackness, despite my inherent identity as a Black man. As a result, I joined the Black Panther Party in college. I needed some validation that I was, indeed, who I appeared to be, not only on the outside but on the inside as well. Both Blacks and whites alike told me that I was "not Black enough" for them (they saw the way I played basketball, muttering "Egads" under my breath with every foul or missed layup—Egads). This applied not only to my physical appearance and manner of speech but also extended to my intellect and my books.My most recent manuscript was denied by every major publisher. From a reviewer: "While somewhat compelling and an interesting take on the retelling of Aeschylus, we just don't see how it relates to the Black experience." Despite my being a Black writer, the book was, apparently, not written from a Black perspective. At the latest New York literary party, a well-known literary agent told me, "You should forget those retellings of yours; classical works aren't what the market is looking for. What we're seeking are the true, gritty stories of Black life—write that, then give me a call."I told him, "My stories are Black stories." And in their own way, it was true. Was I not a Black writer? The agent shuffled past me to attend to a performance artist so they could see what they could do for one another, before never speaking to each other again.I didn't know how to contend with any of it: how to portray myself as "Black enough," the backward, ill-feeling guilt behind not being so, and how to fit into the mold that society made of Black men. We all had to be gangsters, rappers. But why should I have been anything other than who I was? Race was a construct I didn't believe in and rarely dwelt on, until those moments arose when guilt compelled me to see the "other side" of the matter. I saw its real-world consequences: police brutality, discrimination, violence. I didn't know if that meant I was supposed to take part in any of it.

written_by_MFA015.Excerpt2: When I was in college I joined the Black Panther Party. I wore a black turtleneck sweater and black beret and stood outside in the cold with arms full of old newspapers. I wasn’t trying to prove my ideological stance. I was trying to prove that I was indeed Black. It seems that no one, Black or white, thought I was Black enough. Once when a loose ball was bounding about on a basketball court, I muttered “Egads,” and people’s heads turned. When I savored a biscuit and described it as sublime, I received odd looks. Of a retelling of Aeschylus, a reviewer wrote: “The novel has some merit, but do we really need this from a Black man?” A literary agent puffed up with plastic pride told me at a New York party that nobody wanted an intellectual Black man, especially one doing retellings of Greek plays. He glanced across the room at a woman with strings of beads in her otherwise naked Afro, then turned back to me. He said if I gave him a story about cocaine and drive-bys and baby mamas and regrets, he would make me a millionaire. I told him to fuck off and that my life was Black and that the stories I wrote were in fact Black stories. written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: First it was the spotted sickness that unfurled from the south. I was not there, but I remember. Then forced migration westward, to Dakota land, and the Anishinabe signed a treaty. These were made to be broken and to break us. After came more displacements, the government making exiles of us again. So many documents and so much displacement. I lie on my back and these papers press hard on my chest when I think of them. In 1914 it was consumption, creeping slowly through the reservation like woodsmoke. Taking us one by one, and unraveling us, and my family could not escape it either. The Pillagers were unraveled by this new sickness and so was our community, huddled so close together as we were. Unable to escape each other, shoulder, pressed to shoulder, and unable to escape the sickness. I was the only one of us who lived. Nanapush, the sole survivor. For this suffering I am already an elder, but I am only fifty years old. And for this terrible privilege I have been witness to the end of the traditions. I have led the last buffalo hunt, saw the last bear killed. Trapped the last beaver with a mature pelt, and felled the last old birch. Sometimes we understood we were doing these things for the final time. Other times, we didn't realize until after. The loss hurts in my teeth. It lives in my early wrinkles and sore body. But I have saved the Pillager family. When the government comes with more papers, more opportunities to strip us of our land and our identity, I have resisted. I did not sign. I will not sign—we will not be exiles again. Too much has already been taken. The Anishinabe persist, and I will continue to resist for the Pillagers who are lost, and for those of us who carry on.
written_by_MFA026.Excerpt2: Before my life, the Anishinabe were traveling people. We had been on the move for generations. First we went in quest of food, and then in search of land to call home. We fought back the spotted sickness that came to take us from the South, then followed the dragonflies that helped us find Pounded Rice Lake. After that we traveled west to what the Dakotas claimed was nearly across the world. But we lived there. We signed a paper. We put our mark down. We were going to all but vanish onto government-assembled squares of earth.But that failed, for they came to us with more papers. Of every ten who had lived, only five remained. We have a million names for death in Anishinabe culture. Their documents gave death just as many names. They told us to name ourselves over and over again, to give ourselves numbers. Threatened by unknown sicknesses, we rose and ran. We found our way out of our human skins to survive. And still we died.Even after all this, in 1914, something new came to us on the reservation. A slow sickness called consumption. It lodged deep within us, swallowing us bit by bit. Years went by and whole families succumbed. That is what killed the Pillagers, taking their breath away as they slept wrapped in their blankets. Their deaths joined the light strokes of the sunlight on the stump underneath us, the stump of black ash. I alone escaped. At fifty I was considered an old man. I led the last buffalo hunt. I trapped the last beaver with a mature pelt. I saw the last bear killed in our old hunting territories and cut down the last old birch. But I also saved the last Pillager, and refused to be re-numbered or to sign the government papers.
written_by_MFA026.Reason: E2  seems to provide a greater sense of agency to the Anishinabe people at first, whereas E1 only describes the events as things happening to the narrator and his people ("it was the spotted sickness" and "forced migration westward...the government making exiles of us again" and "For this suffering I am already an elder, but I am only fifty years old. And for this terrible privilege I have been witness to the end of the traditions"). There is some movement in decision making for Nanapush with the many lasts that he commences, but this seems to be more out of a reaction to the past being gone than any proactive decisions or agency. E2, on the other hand, is more effective at demonstrating the Anishinabe as people with agency and then demonstrating how that agency is taken away. This makes for a greater emotional depth. Additionally, E2  has much more effective and fluent writing (We found our way out of our human skins to survive. And still we died" and "Their deaths joined the light strokes of the sunlight on the stump underneath us, the stump of black ash").

written_by_MFA007.Excerpt1: First, in the south, we were stormed by the spotted sickness, little red bumps that went from the blanket to the body; then, by the gun, we moved westward to Dakota land, thousands of us dragging our feet across endless miles. Those of us who didn't drop dead from the spots signed a treaty. Before long, we moved once more, condemned to exile, our land taken away by right of the government's stamped document. 1914: Another sickness called 'consumption' rolled in as a terrible storm does, its invisible winds running into our mouths and choking us. After all that, we coughed to our deaths. It came slowly: not like a massacre but like a lost war. We were living six to a room back then, and the cough jumped from one Anishinabe brother to another. The whole Pillager family became ill within a fortnight, the eight of them wasting away in a single room. My whole family went, too. Our tribe, once a tightly woven quilt, unraveled; the knots came loose, the patterns disintegrated into bright threads. Merely fifty years have passed since my birth, yet I am now called an elder, the last of the Nanapush. I remember the end of our lives, the final rites of our traditions. I led the last buffalo hunt. I saw the last bear shot. I trapped the last beaver with a mature pelt. I felled the last birch tree older than a sapling. I remember how, as the sickness razed our people, I went into the room with the eight members of the Pillager family. I fed them water, buffalo meat, and bread. I brought them wet cloths and herbs to ease their fever and coughing. I saved the last of them, the daughter. And I remember receiving the government papers that would rid us of our land and rights. I refused to sign.

written_by_MFA013.Excerpt1: "Can he speak?" one of the lodgers asked, turning away from Hoonie and looking at his mother. Hoonie's parents had received versions of this question time and time again throughout their long lives; Hoonie had been born with a cleft palate and twisted foot, neither of which could be corrected, so his intelligence was often underestimated. "Perhaps you should ask him," Hoonie's mother replied, gesturing to the spot where Hoonie sat. "After all, he is in the room with us." She knew not to be too harsh with her guests, whom their family now relied on for income. To make ends meet, she and her husband, a humble fisherman, had had to vacate the bedroom in their already small home to accommodate more lodgers. They lived in the small fishing village of Yeongdo, near Busan. It was a modest wooden place with sliding paper doors and a clay-tiled roof. To save space, they had even moved their kitchen outside into their vegetable garden. Their landlord in Busan, who had decided to increase their rent without explanation, however lived in a luxurious mansion. "I can speak," Hoonie told the lodger kindly. He had a gentle, thoughtful nature that contrasted with his strong, stocky build. He was mild-mannered enough not to let these sorts of unintended insults bother him. Hoonie's parents were hardworking and pragmatic, and had done their best to raise him. They once had three sons, of whom Hoonie was the eldest, but the other two had not survived. Yet, through hardship and change, their family stayed resilient. When Japan annexed Korea in 1910, their lives changed dramatically, but Hoonie's parents refused to dwell on the shortcomings of the aristocrats who ruled over them. Instead, they remained focused on their immediate concerns, kept their heads low, and provided for one another as best they could. Hoonie stood and bowed toward the lodger, who returned a subtle look of pity, then avoided eye contact altogether. He was always hurt by these small gestures but was far too kind to allow those who hurt him to feel ashamed. It was easier that way.
written_by_MFA013.Excerpt2: In the early years of the twentieth century, an aging fisherman and his wife decided to take in lodgers for extra money. The towering cliffs of Yeongdo, an island beside the bustling port city of Busan, overlooked the sea, and its villagers earned a living by fishing or tending small farms. However, Japan's increasing incursions into the nation's politics and economy had raised taxes, and the fisherman and his wife, like their neighbors, were struggling to get by.The couple worked hard, and over the years they had three sons. But, only their eldest son, Hoonie, survived infancy. Hoonie was born with a cleft palate and a twisted foot, yet he was so stout and strong as a child that his parents couldn't help but sense that the boy was a blessing sent to them. People who didn't know him well assumed he wasn't very bright, so they left him alone, which was what he preferred. What no one noticed right away was that Hoonie had a quick, clever mind and a precocious appetite for learning.In 1910, when Japan annexed Korea, the fisherman and his wife, who had come from Songdo as orphans, did not concern themselves with politics. When the rent was raised again, the household was forced to give up their bedroom to accommodate more lodgers. They swept their quarters clean, did laundry, and made simple meals for the young men who worked in the docks. The elderly couple partitioned off a small corner of the large front room where lodgers normally slept; and after dinner, they unrolled their bedding behind this makeshift wall, sharing the same room as their guests.Eventually they moved their kitchen—consisting of a brick wood-burning stove and a larder—out to the vegetable garden. In the winter, cold wind sent snow and broken maple leaves through the warm papered rooms of their house. Their humble wooden house, with its two rooms, covered porch, and traditional ondol heated floors, was dwarfed by the landlord's opulent Busan mansion, which boasted twenty rooms, imported screens and furniture, and elegant clay-tiled roofing.
written_by_MFA013.Reason:
In terms of how the elements of the scene are ordered, E1 is much more coherent and effective in the way it starts with the in-scene conflict, explains the mistreatment, then goes into the backstory of the family once the dynamic of the scene has been laid down. Once that is in place, E1 does a great job focusing on Hoonie, all culminating in a sad but great line "He was always hurt by these small gestures but was far too kind to allow those who hurt him to feel ashamed. It was easier that way."

E2, on the other hand, isn't as effective as a start because we have to wade through the exposition before we get a sense of conflict, stakes, or care/desire from the family. For that reason, E1 is better in terms of coherence (the ordering of elements) and its transitioning from one topic to another.

written_by_MFA031.Excerpt1: Even before Japan annexed Korea, you could find the greatest expressions of both grief and resilience in small communities like Yeongdo, a small fishing village near Busan. There, a young fisherman found an equally hardworking, pragmatic wife, learned the different catches of the Yellow Sea’s shadowed and sunny areas, lost his country, had three sons, mourned two of them, and grew old. As displacement from military occupation spiked local rents, he and his wife set aside two rooms for lodgers. Despite the objective squalor of their situation and home—a modest wooden structure with a clay-tiled roof—the sliding paper doors of their boarding house became associated with safe harbor, gracious prices in slow fishing seasons, and cooking that made a wife seem unnecessary. When Korea was finally annexed in 1910, they gave up their bedroom, and even their kitchen, for more lodgers. The fishermen boarders relished the sight of the wife, seemingly unphased by the ruling class’s failures and unfolding political catastrophes, in the vegetable garden pickling vegetables and boiling soups with their catches. Over those meals, they got drunk, shouted banned songs from their youth, and mourned their country that the aristocrats had handed to a foreign emperor like a dowry without a groom. Even their landlord, who had kept his luxurious Busan mansion by donating an entire village’s homes to military occupation, came by one day to sample her maeuntang. Hoonie, the couple’s eldest and only surviving son was born with a cleft palate and twisted foot. However, the dire political and bodily circumstances Hoonie was born into instilled a quiet strength and clever adaptability. Some visitors from the mainland mistook his physical appearance and reserved speech for stupidity; his neighbors, though, often said, “Ki Hoonie will figure out with three limbs what you couldn’t with five.” Neighbors admired him as the kindest and most reliable man on the island, even as they decried the lack of marriageable men for their daughters. While his increasingly frail parents grew more desperate for a daughter-in-law, they secretly relished the diligent, undivided care Hoonie gave them and the boarding house.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: The old fisherman and his wife lived in Yeongdo, a small village near Busan. The couple was hardworking and pragmatic, and always sought new ways to bring money into their household. When the income from fish alone was no longer enough to sustain them, they decided to open their home to lodgers. The travelers passed through the village on the way to or back from Busan, and were always in need of a hot meal and a place to sleep. Both the travelers and the fisherman and his wife were happy for the company. As the years went by, the fisherman and his wife had three sons together. Only Hoonie, the eldest, survived. He was born with a cleft palate and a twisted foot. Despite these challenges, Hoonie had a strong, stocky build and a kind, thoughtful nature. His shy voice and reserved manner of speech often caused people to underestimate his intelligence. In the face of teasing and mockery from people in the village, Hoonie remained diligent and mild-mannered. Elsewhere in the country, great turbulence was taking place. In 1910, Japan annexed Korea, and a tremendous political shift occurred. The fisherman and his wife were untroubled by the news. They didn't think it did any good to worry about how their aristocratic rulers had failed them. The decision-makers up in their high, gleaming chairs were as far removed from them as the moon. Meanwhile, there was still work to be done and bills to be paid. To keep up with the rising rent, the fisherman and his wife moved out of their bedroom in order to accommodate more lodgers. They even relocated their kitchen to the vegetable garden to make as much space as possible. Their home was a modest wooden structure with sliding paper doors and a clay-tiled roof. It had been built with the fisherman's own hands shortly before his marriage to his wife. In the heart of Busan, the luxurious mansion of the fisherman's landlord stood proud and stately. It had been assembled by hundreds of hands, and would one day be taken apart by hundreds more.

written_by_MFA003.Excerpt1: It was the next night when my father returned to my little apartment and I, anxious for his arrival, waited at the same wobbling card table on which I wrote the unbound novel he held in his hands. It had taken me two years to write it, and in those two years, my mother had refused to read a page. During one of her morning visits over lukewarm tea, she’d said “If it’s writing you want, I fail to see how work in advertising won’t fulfill you.” It was her tone that foretold that in leaping and striving for these dreams, we may lose sight of the path that had been carved for us long before. But my father read the entire novel. He had asked to. And when he slammed the pages onto my table, in the harsh return to the site of their creation, I was certain he would insist I write no more. I allowed myself to believe that, in the moment of silence after the table steadied, my words were so inept they could not draw near the man who best knew me. I believed this until he embraced me. I did not realize until much later, far beyond the glances of accumulated days behind me, that his momentary silence was the struggle for his own words. “One day,” he eventually said. “One day, my son will be a famous author. A Nobel prize author. One day.” The loose pages on the desk were an off-white bond paper, and it is these pages I have kept and oftentimes return to, long after I titled the manuscript Cevdet Bey and His Sons, long after it was sold and published, long after my relocating to a larger apartment in Istanbul and my father’s passing seven years later in December, 2002. I return to the typed and blue-hashed pages not to read but to see what my father had seen, to see him seeing his son and all his promise.
written_by_MFA003.Excerpt2: Thirty years ago, my father gave me a small suitcase like the one in this image, filled with his manuscripts, and asked me to read them. I held that suitcase in my hand for a full week, imagining its contents and wavering between the melancholy solitude it would bring and my desire not to disappoint my father. Finally, I decided not to open it because I wanted to remain the child of a father who kept a suitcase of secrets. When my first novel "Cevdet Bey and His Sons" was published in Turkey, I was twenty-three, and I gave it to my father to read. Until then, I had never given him any samples of my writing, and that small suitcase had not yet been mentioned between us. Unlike my mother, my father—who was concerned for my welfare but even more for my freedom—did not object to my becoming a novelist. Like all fathers, he wished for his son to have extraordinary success, yet he refrained from making demands, urging me only to be free and happy.I waited, as nervous as my mother was, for my father's reaction after he had finished reading my novel. Finally, when he returned, overcome with excitement, I studied his expression and searched for clues. My father said not a word, but—ignoring my mother and the others—motioned for me to follow him into his study. For a time, we stood across from each other, like two schoolboys who had quarreled, awkwardly unable to speak. Then, embarrassed by his own emotions, he hugged me. When we pulled apart, he looked at me affectionately and said, "You will be a very good writer, bebeğim." He then added, like a true man of his generation, that he expected me to one day win the prize I am receiving today. I recount this here proudly, yet with some embarrassment—and his supposition has come true.My dear father died in December 2002.
written_by_MFA003.Reason:
Excerpt 2 is written in a smooth and narratively engaging way, with lines like "Finally, I decided not to open it because I wanted to remain the child of a father who kept a suitcase of secrets" and "Until then, I had never given him any samples of my writing, and that small suitcase had not yet been mentioned between us."
Meanwhile, Excerpt 1 is adequate but full of cliche and bland, overworked language, like " It was her tone that foretold that in leaping and striving for these dreams, we may lose sight of the path that had been carved for us long before."

written_by_MFA010.Excerpt2: Sitting down to reflect on my life makes everything fall silent around me. I remember that I had committed to becoming a novelist at a very young age. My domestic circumstances were somewhat fortunate: although my mother believed I could commit myself to more useful professions like law and medicine, my father had always supported my ambition to become a writer. But one memory of my father is more significant than the rest. I remember that when, as a young man, I wrote my first novel, “Cevdet Bay and His Sons,” I sent a copy to my father for his opinion. Till I heard back from him, my days were consumed by the anxiety of what he might have to say. I came to care for my father’s opinion and approval more than anyone else’s. I had been waiting for my father to return home. I wanted to know his thoughts. On the day of his arrival, I stood by the door of our house and looked at him like I was nothing more than a child. My father must have understood what I was asking him. He walked up to me and embraced me. Although he didn’t say a word, I understood that he approved of my manuscript. For a few days, my father refused to talk about the manuscript but later, one cold evening, he expressed a strong and optimistic confidence about my future writing career. Like a proud father he said "Aslanım olacaksın." He didn’t name a prize but he predicted that I would go on to receive a prestigious one. When my father died in 2002, I looked outside the window and imagined that door by which I stood waiting for him and remembered his words of encouragement. Sometimes, when I am alone, I still feel the warmth of that embrace.

written_by_MFA016.Excerpt1: I had given it to him at last, my first novel, “Cevdet Bey and His Sons,” and I waited with equal parts fear and excitement for his reaction to it. The book took me several years to complete and the time had not come easily; my mother had not supported the endeavor and took every opportunity to disparage this sodden “waste of youth” while my father quietly, gently, encouraged me with small gifts and an allowance. I knew better than to try convincing my mother, though those modern writers who I hoped to emulate in the West had taken a similar commitment to writing, she did not respect them, and would not want me to achieve a similar goal to any of theirs. I saw my father from across the boiled asphalt lot and felt my fears realized in his step—would he join my mother after reading my manuscript? I rose from my car to meet him. I searched for a hint of his answer in his gait or his eyes and saw nothing but the movements and recognition of an animal. Perhaps my father’s support ended now, perhaps I had failed him, perhaps this moment would end this chapter of my life and its purpose. All my anxieties melted when we embraced. He surged toward me as we met, pumping his arms to pat me on the back with reverent enthusiasm, then pulling me close to his chest as he had when I was a child, and I felt his pride. He held me out in front of him and smiled. “You will succeed, my son,” he said. “You will win prestigious prizes and teach somewhere.” It is this memory I cling to after his death in 2002—how he remained such a father to me.
